noteRef.topicTitle: Structure and functions in living organisms

specPoints.text: understand the sources, roles and effects of the following hormones: ADH, FSH and LH

primer.text: You already met insulin and adrenaline as chemical messengers. This note adds three more: ADH, the kidney's water valve; and the reproductive pair FSH and LH, which run the menstrual cycle from the pituitary gland. For each one, learn source, role and effect — the summary table's three columns are the exam's checklist.

lessons.title: ADH: the water-content controller
lessons.opening: ADH (antidiuretic hormone) comes from the pituitary gland and answers one question — how concentrated is the blood? Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus sense the solute level: too concentrated means more ADH, which makes the nephrons' collecting ducts leakier, so more water returns to the blood and the urine shrinks to a small, concentrated volume.
keyPoints: ADH is released by the pituitary gland and controls the water content of the blood.
Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus monitor how concentrated the blood solutes are.
Low blood water means more ADH, leakier collecting ducts and more water reabsorbed.
The result is a smaller volume of concentrated urine when water is scarce.
High blood water reverses everything — less ADH, less reabsorption, plentiful dilute urine.

low.restatement: Low water: hypothalamus senses it, pituitary sends ADH, ducts get leakier, blood reclaims water, urine shrinks and concentrates.
low.analogy: ADH is the tap handle on the kidney's drain — twist it shut when water is precious, open it wide when there is surplus.
low.examPointer: Chain the sequence in order — hypothalamus, pituitary, collecting duct, urine — chain marks are standard here.

medium.restatement: ADH's effect is a permeability change: the hormone alters collecting-duct water permeability, so reabsorption tracks the blood's osmotic state detected by hypothalamic osmoreceptors.
medium.analogy: Imagine adjustable sieves — the hormone sets how fine the mesh is, deciding how much water drains away.
medium.examPointer: Name the detecting cells (osmoreceptors) and the acting structure (collecting ducts) — both earn separate marks.

options.explanation: The pituitary releases ADH on hypothalamic instruction.
The pancreas releases insulin, not ADH.
That gland releases adrenaline.
Ovaries release oestrogen and progesterone.

check.stem: Which cells detect that the blood is too concentrated?

options.explanation: Hypothalamic osmoreceptors monitor blood solute concentration.
Duct cells obey ADH; they do not sense the blood first.
Those detect light, not solutes.
External taste has nothing to do with blood monitoring.

check.stem: What does ADH change in the nephron?

options.text: The permeability of the collecting ducts to water
options.explanation: ADH makes the collecting ducts more or less water-permeable.
No such effect is described.
Nephron count is fixed.
Sweat glands are unrelated to ADH here.

check.stem: After drinking a large volume of water, what happens?

options.text: Less ADH is released, so a large volume of dilute urine forms
options.explanation: Dilute blood suppresses ADH and reabsorption falls.

options.text: More ADH is released, producing concentrated urine
options.explanation: That response would worsen the dilution.
Monitoring continues either way.
Structures persist; only permeability changes.

check.stem: Which urine output matches a dehydrated person?

options.text: A large volume of very dilute urine
options.explanation: That wastes water the body needs.
Production continues, just reduced.

options.text: A small volume of concentrated urine
options.explanation: More reabsorption shrinks and concentrates the urine.
The whole point of ADH is to shift concentration.

check.stem: Give the full name and the source gland of ADH.
check.modelAnswer: Antidiuretic hormone, released by the pituitary gland.

check.stem: State the two urine changes when blood water is too low.
check.modelAnswer: A smaller volume of urine that is more concentrated.

check.stem: Explain why concentrated blood leads to concentrated urine.
check.modelAnswer: Concentrated blood means water is scarce; hypothalamic osmoreceptors detect this and the pituitary releases more ADH, which raises the collecting ducts' permeability, so more of the filtrate's water returns to the blood — leaving less water behind, hence a small, concentrated urine.

check.stem: An athlete drinks nothing during a marathon and sweats heavily. Predict the ADH signal, the duct response and the urine.
check.modelAnswer: Blood water falls, so hypothalamic osmoreceptors signal for maximal ADH release; the collecting ducts become highly permeable and reabsorb as much water as possible; the athlete produces only a small volume of concentrated urine.

lessons.title: FSH, LH and the menstrual cycle
sourceHeadings: Hormonal control of the menstrual cycle
The roles of FSH and LH
lessons.opening: Four hormones steer the menstrual cycle: oestrogen and progesterone prepare and hold the uterus lining, while the pituitary's FSH and LH run the egg's timetable. FSH matures an egg in the ovary and switches on oestrogen release; once oestrogen peaks, LH surges, triggers ovulation, and sets progesterone flowing.
keyPoints: FSH leaves the pituitary gland and starts an egg maturing in the ovary.
FSH also prompts the ovaries to begin releasing oestrogen.
When oestrogen reaches its peak, the pituitary is stimulated to release LH.
LH causes ovulation and stimulates the ovary to produce progesterone.
Oestrogen rebuilds the uterus lining after menstruation; progesterone maintains it for possible pregnancy.

low.restatement: Pituitary signals (FSH then LH) drive the ovary: FSH matures the egg and starts oestrogen, LH pops the egg and starts progesterone.
low.analogy: FSH is the coach who trains the athlete (egg); LH is the starting gun that sends her out and hands the baton to progesterone.
low.examPointer: Keep the two pituitary hormones separate — FSH matures, LH releases; swapping them is the classic error.

medium.restatement: The cycle is a hormone relay: rising oestrogen from FSH-stimulated ovaries feeds back to trigger the LH surge, so ovulation follows the peak — each gland's output becomes the next gland's instruction.
medium.analogy: Like passing notes in class: each message tells the next sender when to write, and the timetable never stalls.
medium.examPointer: Anchor each hormone to a source — pituitary for FSH and LH, ovaries for oestrogen, corpus luteum for progesterone.

check.stem: What does FSH cause in the ovary?

options.explanation: FSH causes an egg to begin maturing in the ovary.
Release (ovulation) is LH's doing.
That is oestrogen's job.
Adrenaline belongs to a different gland entirely.
The oestrogen peak stimulates the pituitary to release LH.
Progesterone is not the LH trigger named here.

options.text: The egg already having been released
options.explanation: LH causes the release, not follows it.
That triggers ADH, not LH.
LH releases the egg and stimulates progesterone output.
Maturation is FSH's role.
Menstruation is not LH's named effect.
That belongs to the pancreas.

check.stem: Which hormone maintains the uterus lining during pregnancy?

options.explanation: Progesterone maintains the thick lining for possible pregnancy.
FSH matures eggs.
ADH manages blood water.
Adrenaline readies the body for danger.

check.stem: In which gland are FSH and LH both produced?

options.explanation: Both are pituitary hormones.
Ovaries make oestrogen and progesterone.
The hypothalamus detects; the pituitary releases.
The liver stores glucose here, not hormones.

check.stem: State the source and role of FSH.
check.modelAnswer: Released by the pituitary gland; it causes an egg to mature and stimulates oestrogen release.

check.stem: State the source and role of LH.
check.modelAnswer: Released by the pituitary gland; it causes ovulation and stimulates progesterone production.

check.stem: Explain why the oestrogen peak matters for the cycle's timing.
check.modelAnswer: The oestrogen peak is the signal that the egg is ready: it stimulates the pituitary to release LH, and LH triggers ovulation — so the peak converts the ovary's readiness into the precise moment of release, timing the cycle correctly.

check.stem: A fertility drug boosts FSH levels. Predict the chain of hormonal events that follows.
check.modelAnswer: Extra FSH matures more eggs and pushes the ovaries to release more oestrogen; the elevated oestrogen stimulates the pituitary to release LH, which can trigger ovulation — and the ovary responds by producing progesterone afterwards.

glossary.definition: Antidiuretic hormone from the pituitary gland that raises collecting-duct permeability so more water is reabsorbed.
Hypothalamus cells that detect the concentration of solutes in the blood.
Follicle-stimulating hormone from the pituitary that matures an egg and switches on oestrogen release.
Luteinising hormone from the pituitary that triggers ovulation and progesterone production.
